newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA TO INVITE BIDDERS FOR CHEMICAL PLANT.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA TO INVITE BIDDERS FOR CHEMICAL PLANT.

text.p: Bulgaria plans to offer for sale a 60 percent stake in its chemical fertiliser producer Himko by the year-end, a senior official said.

The executive director of the Privatisation Agency Vesselin Blagoev said a privatisation procedure offering 60 percent of the Vratsa-based chemical giant would be opened in the middle of December at the earliest.

Blagoev said the agency was now in a process of clarifying whether a few railways which Himko uses were part of the national railway network and if so the agency would need more time to write off their value from the plant's capital.

"I think we can invite bidders in the middle of December at the earliest," Blagoev told a news conference on return from a visit to London where he carried out a marketing campaign aimed at attracting the interest of potential investors in Bulgaria's sell-offs.
"We can expect to finalise the deal by the end of the first quarter of 1997," he added.
Himko is the second chemical firm after calcinated soda producer Sodi-Devnya to be offered for sale among other 20 major state enterprises which the government hopes to sell in the short term.
The plant, which exports 92 percent of its products, had a net profit of 60 million levs for 1994.
Himko, which imports 64 percent of its raw materials, raised revenue from export sales for the first nine months of 1996 by $10 million to $107 million over the same period last year.
In lev terms, pre-tax profit doubled to 7.3 billion levs for the same period but the currency has fallen from 70 to the dollar at the beginning of the year to about 360 now.
Himko has 20 installations, including for reforming, carbamide, carbon sulphide, carbon dioxide and a catalytic installation.

Earlier this year Himko set up a joint venture with Frankfurt-based Messer Grieshelm GmbH, a subsidiary of Germany's Hoechst , to distribute industrial gases in the region. Himko has 49 percent and the Germans have the remaining stake.
